data.title: Everyone drinks from the same reservoir
data.concept: Shared database or a database per service: consistency, availability, and who owns the truth.
data.voice: Sixteen engineers, one schema, and a migrations channel nobody mutes.
data.briefing: Every team writes to the shared Postgres, and at peak it is the busiest reservoir in town. Orders are heading for 2,600 a day, and the shared Postgres was sized for fewer. One more migration that locks the orders table and checkout stops.
data.dilemma: Who owns the order data, and how much inconsistency are you willing to live with to keep taking orders?
data.disagreement: Experts disagree here. Richardson and Helland argue that each service should own its data and accept eventual consistency, because distributed transactions do not scale. Others reply that one well-run Postgres beats a fleet of small ones until the team is much larger, and that 'eventually' is a hard word to say to an auditor. Brewer himself says the CAP choice comes up only during a partition, not as a permanent label.
data.readNext: Read Brewer's twelve-years-later essay first: CAP is a choice you make during a partition, not a label. Then Helland on life without distributed transactions, Richardson's chapter on sagas, and the transactions and replication chapters of Kleppmann.

scale-the-reservoir.title: Keep the shared Postgres; buy a bigger one and a read replica
scale-the-reservoir.optimizes: One source of truth, real transactions, no migration this quarter.
scale-the-reservoir.costs: Every team stays coupled through one schema; replica reads go stale at times. The bill arrives later.

split-the-reservoir.title: orders-db of its own, with domain events
split-the-reservoir.optimizes: Orders keep flowing when the shared reservoir struggles; the orders team owns its schema.
split-the-reservoir.costs: A data migration now, eventual consistency forever, and reconciliation jobs to prove it adds up.

coordinate-transactions.title: Two databases, one two-phase commit
coordinate-transactions.optimizes: Split storage that still commits as one transaction.
coordinate-transactions.costs: Latency on every order and a coordinator that blocks both stores when either one stalls.

events.series-a: Series A closed. Two years of runway and a board that now asks about 'platform'.
events.reservoir-dry: Tuesday, 19:40. The shared Postgres runs out of connections. Checkout, catalog and payouts all wait in the same line.

inspections.shared-reservoir: Site inspection: the shared reservoir is still the busiest in town. Forty tables, five teams, no owner on most of them. Three migrations are queued for Thursday's window.

review.who-owns-truth: Where does the truth about an order live now, and what consistency did you promise the rest of the system?
review.what-goes-stale: What can now be stale, slow or blocked, and what did you give up to get the rest?
review.when-to-split: What would make you split (or merge back) the data, and what number would tell you?

rubric.grounded-context: The context names the constraints that actually shaped the choice (team, traffic, runway, regulation).
rubric.names-consistency: The decision says what consistency the system now offers: transactional, eventual, or stale reads, and where.
rubric.names-tradeoff: The consequences name at least one force that got worse, not only the ones that got better.
rubric.names-given-up: What was given up is written down in a full sentence.
rubric.revisit-trigger: The revisit trigger is a condition someone could notice, not a hope.

data.scaleKeepsShipping: A larger instance and a replica take days of operations work and no application rewrite, so feature work continues.
data.scaleBiggerBox: A bigger primary plus a replica roughly doubles the database bill, which is still smaller than a new service's infrastructure.
data.scaleStaleReads: Asynchronous replicas lag by seconds at peak; some customers will not see the order they just placed if the page reads from the replica.
data.scaleCouplingGrows: With every team writing to the same schema, a column rename becomes a negotiation, and the coupling compounds with each new table.
data.scaleMigrationQueue: Schema changes queue behind one shared migration window; people spend time learning which team's tables they must not touch.
data.scaleHeadroom: Doubling capacity buys about a year of growth at current rates, enough to absorb the first peak that runs out of connections.
data.scaleOneAuditTrail: One database with real transactions gives an auditor one consistent history, without reconciling stores.
data.splitMigration: Moving orders to their own database means dual writes, a backfill and a cut-over: about a quarter of one team's time.
data.splitMovingParts: A second database, a queue, an outbox and idempotent consumers: more parts that can each fail on their own.
data.splitEventual: Once orders and the rest live in different stores, every engineer has to reason about states that are true here and not yet there.
data.splitInfrastructure: A second managed database and a queue, with their environments and backups, from the first month.
data.splitReconciliation: Eventual consistency needs proof: nightly reconciliation jobs and someone who reads their output.
data.splitAutonomy: Once the cut-over is done, the orders team changes its schema and deploys without asking four other teams.
data.splitStaysOpen: When the shared Postgres saturates, orders still commit to their own store and the rest catches up from events.
data.splitAuditAcrossStores: An auditor wants one consistent picture of each order. Reconstructing it from two stores and an event log is slow and expensive.
data.txStillAtomic: Two-phase commit keeps an order and its stock change atomic across both databases: no orphans, no reconciliation jobs.
data.txRoundTrips: Each order now pays a prepare round and a commit round across the network while locks are held; everything touching orders gets slower to build and to run.
data.txCoordinatorIsCritical: The coordinator becomes infrastructure every order depends on, with its own log, recovery and failure modes.
data.txInfrastructure: A second database and a highly available coordinator, paid from the first month.
data.txInDoubt: When the coordinator fails between prepare and commit, transactions stay in doubt with locks held, and someone on call has to resolve them by hand.
data.txBlocksInPartition: Two-phase commit picks consistency over availability: when one participant is slow, prepared locks hold and both stores stall together.
data.txAuditFriendly: One atomic commit per order across both stores is easy to show an auditor.
data.seriesARunway: The Series A adds about two years of runway at the current burn.
data.reservoirDryPeak: At about 2,600 orders a day, peak-hour connections exceed what the shared Postgres can serve and every team's queries wait together.

postgres-replica.name: Postgres read replica
postgres-replica.role: copy of the reservoir, a few seconds behind
